posts.central_knowledge_unit: Ulama, a 3,400-year-old ballgame that survived in Mexico | AP News
posts.claim: Ulama de cadera is a living Sinaloan hip-ball variant that scholarship and Mexico’s cultural-heritage inventory characterize as a continuation of the Mesoamerican ballgame tradition. Its players use the hip/upper leg and a heavy natural-rubber ball. The approximately 3,400-year date is securely supported for an early formal Mesoamerican ballcourt at Paso de la Amada, not for a demonstrated 3,400-year unchanged history of the present-day Sinaloan game.

posts.claim: The ballgame represents one of the most enduring and iconic features of ancient Mesoamerican civilization, yet its origins and evolution remain poorly understood, primarily associated with the Gulf Coast and southern Pacific coastal lowlands. While one early ballcourt dates to 1650 BCE from the Chiapas lowlands, ballcourts have remained undocumented in the Mesoamerican highlands until a millennium later, suggesting less involvement by highland civilizations in the ballgame’s evolution.
